robustness.from: WEAKEST ROW IN THIS BATCH - two explicit caveats. (1) POPULATION IS MIXED, not strictly healthy: the pooled estimate combines community/healthy adults with 'vulnerable populations' (subgroup Hedges' g = 0.414) and participants with baseline vitamin D deficiency (g = 0.480), plus a no-biological-flaws subgroup at g = 0.549. Because the effect concentrates in deficient/vulnerable strata, the true effect in replete healthy adults is almost certainly SMALLER than 0.128 - this row should be filtered out of any healthy-adults-only analysis. (2) NO CI CAPTURED: the 95% CI for the pooled g = 0.128 is not reported in the abstract and the Neuropsychology Review full text is paywalled; only p = .008 is available. CI left null deliberately rather than back-computed from p - do NOT impute it. Effect was confined to global cognition; no significant effect in any specific cognitive domain (memory, executive, attention, processing speed). Preregistered PROSPERO CRD42021249908. In a strictly cognitively-healthy population Cochrane (Rutjes 2018, PMID:30556597) found no effect of vitamin D3 + calcium (1 trial, 4143 participants, MD -0.1 MMSE points, 95% CI -0.81 to 0.61) over a mean 7.8 y. Sign already oriented so positive = pro-cognitive; no sign flip applied.
robustness.to: INTERVAL NOT RECOVERABLE 2026-09-20: source is fully closed access and reports no interval in its abstract (only Hedges g = 0.128, p = .008). Not in PMC, not in Europe PMC (isOpenAccess=false), no preprint. Population is also not clean-healthy (mean age 65.2, 78.5% women, non-demented but not screened healthy-young).

robustness.from: WEAKEST ROW IN THIS BATCH — include only with the following caveats. (1) NO CONFIDENCE INTERVAL is reported in the abstract; ci_reported=false and bounds left null rather than estimated. (2) The number of pooled STUDIES (k) is not stated; the abstract reports 104 individual effect sizes, which is an effect-size count not a study count, so n_studies is null rather than guessed. (3) The AUTHORS THEMSELVES DISOWN the pooled estimate: the abstract states this effect size 'was not representative of the 104 individual effect sizes reported' — i.e. severe heterogeneity, so d=0.56 should not be treated as a stable population estimate. (4) Vintage 2004, pre-PRISMA, Hedges & Olkin 1985 procedures, no risk-of-bias or publication-bias assessment mentioned. (5) No PMID exists (journal not PubMed-indexed at the time); DOI supplied and verified against the Cambridge University Press record. (6) Population health status not explicitly stated. Sign already pro-cognitive-positive, no flip. Secondary finding: larger effects for memory than non-memory tasks; unexpectedly NO greater benefit in older vs younger adults.
